extraction.title: Universal multilayer network exploration by random walk with restart
extraction.document_type: Journal research article (open access, CC BY 4.0), with methods and supplementary material referenced but supplementary notes not in the extracted text
extraction.coverage: Read all 1277 lines of the extracted text (abstract, introduction, results including the RWR formalism, numerical implementation, LOOCV and link-prediction evaluations, parameter-space exploration, discussion, data/code availability, figure captions, references 1-34, back matter). Supplementary Notes 1-5 and Figs S9-S16 are cited but not in the file, so their contents are not covered. Metadata hint corrected: full author list is Anthony Baptista, Aitor Gonzalez, Anais Baudot; article number 170.
extraction.research_question: Can random walk with restart (RWR) be generalized to explore any combination of multiplex, monoplex and bipartite networks (a "universal multilayer network"), and how do added network layers and bipartite links change prediction performance and the stability of outputs to input parameters?
extraction.theory: Random walks as iterative stochastic processes on graphs; RWR as a steady-state diffusion / personalized PageRank measuring proximity of all nodes to seed(s) (p.1-2, citing Lovasz 1993, Brin and Page 1998, Gomez et al. 2013). Multilayer formalism following De Domenico et al. 2013 and Kivela et al. 2014: supra-adjacency matrices for multiplex layers (with inter-layer jump probability delta), bipartite matrices for heterogeneous links, and a column-normalized supra-heterogeneous transition matrix with inter-network jump probabilities lambda and restart parameters eta (network) and tau (layer) (Eqs 5-16, Fig. 2, p.2-4). No behavioural or social theory is used.
extraction.data: Two empirical multilayer networks, no sample sizes given in the main text. (1) Biological network: a gene multiplex (gene physical and functional relationships), a drug multiplex (drug clinical and chemical relationships), and a disease monoplex (phenotypic similarity), linked by gene-disease, drug-gene and drug-disease bipartite networks (p.4, detailed in Supplementary Note 3.B). Unit: genes, drugs, diseases as nodes. (2) Airports network: French, British and German airport multiplex networks (nodes = airports; edges = national flight connections for three airline companies), linked by French-German, British-German and French-British transnational bipartite networks (p.4, Supplementary Note 3.A). Node and edge counts, time period and original sources are not stated in the main text. Data and code are on OSF (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/ZSMUA) and GitHub (anthbapt/multixrank). Comparison dataset in Methods: the PPI network (p.4-5).
extraction.method: Formal: derivation of RWR on universal multilayer networks (Eqs 1-16), with the normalization generalized from Li and Patra 2010 and Valdeolivas et al. 2018 to N multiplex networks. Implemented as the Python package MultiXrank (optimized, pip installable; complexity analysis in Supplementary Note 2). Evaluation: (a) Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV): each known gene-disease association left out in turn, remaining associations used as seeds, rank of left-out gene recorded and CDF of ranks plotted (p.4-5, Fig. 3a-b). (b) Link Prediction (LP): a gene-disease edge removed and its gene ranked with the disease as seed (p.6, Figs S11, S14). (c) Controls: artificially added transit drug nodes linking gene-disease pairs (1, 2 or 5 per association; Fig 3c-d) and progressive random rewiring of the enhanced bipartite networks (p.5-6). (d) Parameter-space exploration: 125 parameter sets; pairwise similarity of rank output between parameter sets (Eqs 17-18, rank-based distance normalized across multiplex networks), PCA projection, k-means on first two PCs, comparison of top-5 and top-100 nodes per cluster (p.6-8, Fig. 4).
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. Predictive performance is assessed against held-out known associations (LOOCV and LP). Causal-style claims about bipartite overlap are made by artificially manipulating bipartite connectivity (transit nodes) and then randomizing edges (p.5-6). Stability of outputs is assessed by varying parameters across 125 sets (p.7).
extraction.scope: Methodological paper. Two example networks only: a biological gene/drug/disease network and a three-country airport network. No population or institution; the airport network is a current-era transport network and the biological network is drawn from unspecified databases. Claims of general applicability (social, economic, ecological networks, p.8) are not tested in the paper.

key_findings.finding: RWR is generalized to universal multilayer networks by a column-normalized supra-heterogeneous transition matrix, with inter-multiplex jump parameters lambda and restart parameters eta and tau. The normalization is the step the authors describe as previously unsolved beyond two heterogeneous multiplex networks.
key_findings.location: Results, Eqs 10-16, p.3-4; Introduction p.2 (normalization unsolved for N multiplex networks)
key_findings.numbers: Parameters delta, lambda, eta, tau; sum of lambda over alpha = 1 for each beta; sum over j of tau_kj = 1

key_findings.finding: In the gene-disease LOOCV, combining the gene multiplex with the disease monoplex improves ranking over PPI alone and over the gene multiplex alone. Adding the drug multiplex does not further improve performance.
key_findings.numbers: No numeric values given in text; comparison is by CDF curves

key_findings.finding: In the airports network, adding the German multiplex (with French-German and British-German bipartites) increases RWR's ability to predict French-British airport associations, unlike the drug addition in the biological network.
key_findings.numbers: Three networks: French, British, German airport multiplexes

key_findings.finding: Bipartite overlap explains the difference: only 23% of genes in the gene-disease bipartite network appear in the drug-gene bipartite, and only 5% of diseases appear in the disease-drug bipartite. The airport bipartites show high overlap.
key_findings.numbers: 23% genes; 5% diseases

key_findings.finding: Artificially adding transit drug nodes that link existing gene-disease associations raises LOOCV performance drastically, and the same holds for the airport network.
key_findings.numbers: 1, 2 or 5 transit nodes per gene-disease association (biological); 1, 2 or 5 transit German nodes per French-British association (airports); no performance values in text

key_findings.finding: Progressively randomizing the enhanced bipartite networks continuously lowers LOOCV performance, down to the level of using only two multiplex networks.
key_findings.numbers: Randomization runs to completely random bipartite networks; no values in text

key_findings.finding: Link prediction gives behaviour similar to LOOCV.

key_findings.finding: Output sensitivity to input parameters differs by network. Top-ranked gene nodes vary more than top-ranked disease nodes across 125 parameter sets. The biological gene-disease network has stable regions, while the airport network has highly variable top-rankings.

limitations: Paper has no dedicated limitations section; limitations stated in text: the formalism for some universal networks 'might sometimes require some adaptations' (Discussion, p.7).
Billion-scale networks are not handled; the authors name BEAR (exact or approximate) and BEPI (approximate) as strategies to consider (Discussion, p.8).
Performance on the biological network depends on bipartite overlap, which is low for drug-gene and disease-drug links (23% and 5%) (p.5-6).
Parameter-space stability differs by network (airport network variable; biological network stable in some regions) (p.8).
Only two example networks are evaluated (p.4-8).

summary_md:
Baptista, Gonzalez and Baudot (2022) extend random walk with restart (RWR, a seed-personalized PageRank) to "universal" multilayer networks. These combine any number of multiplex networks, where the same nodes appear on several layers, linked by bipartite networks. They build one column-normalized supra-heterogeneous transition matrix with separate dials for layer jumps (delta), jumps between networks (lambda) and restart allocation (eta, tau). The method ships as the MultiXrank Python package.

They test it with leave-one-out ranking (LOOCV) and link prediction on two examples: a gene/drug/disease network and a three-country airport network. In the biological network, adding the drug multiplex did not help. The cause was low bipartite overlap: only 23% of genes and 5% of diseases are shared across the bipartite links. In the airport network, adding the German layer did help, because overlap there is high. Adding artificial transit nodes raised performance, and gradually randomizing those links lowered it again. Across 125 parameter sets, top-ranked outputs were stable in parts of the biological network and very unstable in the airport network.

Three parts of Paul's system are close to this. The staffer network's layer-balanced PageRank already runs a random walk over several layers: each node splits its transition mass equally across its active layers, and teleport is balanced across entity kinds. However, it checks sensitivity only on damping (0.70/0.85/0.95), never on how mass is split across layers. The Congress multilayer builder merges the cosponsor, engagement, HCoI, social and co-appearance layers into a single edge weight, so it has no layer-jump parameter. No held-out test checks whether each added layer improves anything; the only per-layer evidence is null neighbour co-movement on the cosponsor and HCoI layers. The paper's main lesson for this system is to test whether each layer earns its place, and how much its links overlap with the base graph, before treating more layers as more signal. It gives no evidence about legislatures, lobbying or social ties.

bearings.paper_claim: Top-ranked nodes can shift as walk parameters change, so stability must be measured for each network rather than assumed. The 125-parameter-set exploration was run on the biological gene and disease network only. Airport top-rankings were highly variable in a supplementary figure (Fig S15) with no parameter-set count stated.
bearings.paper_location: Parameter space exploration p.6-8, Eqs 17-18, Fig. 4a-c; airport result stated p.8 citing Supplementary Fig S15
bearings.system_side: Confirmed: a bidirectional row-stochastic walk where each node gives 1/active_layers of its mass to each active layer, split by weight within the layer. Teleport is equal across node kinds. PageRank runs at damping 0.70, 0.85 and 0.95 with L1 distance and top-1000 overlap against 0.85. The equal-layer split is labelled an explicit modeling prior in graph_build.py, not in network_math.py.

The paper says overlap might explain this. Randomizing the boosted bipartite links pushed LOOCV back to the two-network baseline. The authors conclude that more network data is not always better.

bearings.system_side: Confirmed: engagement, HCoI, social and co-appearance (holistic only) layers are merged into one edge weight in fec/network/build_multilayer_network.py. Under the CU config (MEDIA_ADMIT untied) media edges are admitted only for untied pairs and HCoI only for cosponsor-isolated members. Under the holistic config (dominance) a tied pair takes the max weight and its layer tag gains the channel. Social reinforcement of existing ties (factor 1 + 0.3 times min(1, p/0.10)) applies under both configs, not only CU. Layer tags are written to a Provenance sheet (build_multilayer_network.py:200). That sheet is read by fec/legislation/leg_evidence_recompute.py and fec/surfaces/build_dashboard_bundle.py, so the claim that the engine never reads it is wrong. A repo search of fec/network, fec/stance and fec/staffer_network found no LOOCV, link-prediction or held-out test of layer gain.

bearings.paper_claim: RWR scores proximity by summing over walks rather than taking a single path, and RWR has been shown to outperform local distance measures for gene-disease prioritization (Kohler et al. 2008, ref 21). The paper defines RWR as steady-state proximity from all nodes to the seed but does not use the phrase summing over all walks.
bearings.paper_location: Introduction p.2 (ref 21); Results p.2-4 for the RWR definition
bearings.system_side: Confirmed: the template uses a max-product Dijkstra (distToTarget multiplies passive probabilities and keeps the maximum), which orders paths the same way as a shortest path on -log p, though not literally on -log p. ASKM=0.07 and chainHold as the product of activeP along the chain are confirmed. bestSponsors ranks by chainHold, then cost, as stated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: An RWR score seeded at the target, or at the pro-sponsor set, would add a multi-route robustness measure beside the single best chain. The paper's support comes from biological prioritization, not recruitment, and gives no congressional estimate. Any such score is a heuristic proximity, never an ask-success or access probability (D-025).
bearings.verifier_note: Summing over all walks is a standard gloss of RWR but not the paper's wording. The -log p wording is corrected to max-product. The recommendation is a suggestion only.

Coverage: the extracted text has 1277 lines, matching ext.coverage. Paul markup has 34 highlights, none with a note; not separately verified beyond that count.
gaps_exposed: No per-layer held-out evaluation, such as leave-one-out or link prediction, of whether the engagement, HCoI, social or co-appearance layers improve any prediction over the cosponsor-only graph. The builder logs admission counts, not predictive gain.

No measure of overlap or connectivity between the media layers and the cosponsor base. This is the quantity the paper says decides whether a layer helps. Recorded media shares (1.5% of holistic pairs vs 28.8% of CU pairs) are admission statistics, not an overlap test.
The Congress multilayer graph is merged into one weight per pair, so there is no per-layer walk or jump parameter and no way to switch a layer's contribution up or down without a rebuild.

The staffer PageRank sensitivity harness varies only damping. The equal-active-layer split and the per-kind teleport split, both called modelling priors, are never swept or checked for top-k stability.
No randomization control: rewiring a layer's edges to check that its contribution is structural rather than an artifact of density.
flags: Do not read 'more network data is not always better' as support for dropping regular cosponsorship edges. That proposal was measured and REJECTED in this project, and the paper's claim concerns whole added layers with low bipartite overlap, not edge classes within the cosponsor layer.

The paper's column normalization is the standard stochastic normalization of a walk operator, as in the staffer layer_balanced_transition. It is not per-edge volume normalization of cosponsorship weights, which was measured and REJECTED. Do not cite this paper for it.

If RWR or PageRank outputs are adopted anywhere (staffer connectedness, recruitment proximity, stance imputation), they are heuristic model outputs and never closeness, access or introduction probabilities (D-025). Any rank figure must name its window and denominator.
Any claimed gain from adding layers or switching to RWR stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). The paper's own evidence is limited to biology and airport networks.
paul_alignment: Paul's annotations record no takeaways for this paper. Both bibliography entries list it as citation-only, in the Path-Finding Algorithums folder, with only a title-level cross-reference to multilayer social-graph exploration. The one substantive position is a highlight, attached to melange-sna.multilayer-social-press-edges, that more layers are not always better. The paper supports that reading, and it is more relevant now than Paul's note suggests. Since he read it, the system has added several media layers and a holistic co-appearance layer through max or dominance admission without any per-layer predictive test. His filing it under path-finding fits a proximity-ranking alternative to single best-path Dijkstra, but nothing in his notes connects it to the staffer layer-balanced PageRank, which is the closest built analogue.

extraction.research_question: How can social network analysis (SNA) be used to study information exchange, and what does it offer information professionals (for example, librarians and information providers) for assessing and changing information routes and services?
extraction.theory: Relational or network view of social structure: structure is derived empirically from observed relationships rather than from a priori classes (Wellman; Wasserman & Faust). Strength-of-weak-ties argument (Granovetter 1973). Structural holes and brokerage (Burt 1992a). Legitimation of information through close, reciprocated ties (Coleman, Katz & Menzel 1966). Graph theory is the formal base.
extraction.data: None. The article has no sample, unit of analysis, N or observation period. Numerical content is illustrative or cited from other studies: a hypothetical health-information example; the arithmetic of n(n-1) possible ties (n=20 gives 380 links per relationship); Granovetter's job-search sample (over 80% vs under 17%); Wellman et al.'s East York egocentric findings; Haythornthwaite, Wellman & Mantei (1995) with 24 relationships reduced to six dimensions; Wegener (1991) with 11 measures reduced to three attributes.
extraction.method: Narrative review and conceptual synthesis. It sets out SNA principles (relationships, ties, content, direction, strength; egocentric vs whole networks), five network principles (cohesion, structural equivalence, prominence, range, brokerage), and measurement techniques (graph and matrix representation, density, centralization, cliques, degree, closeness, betweenness, block modelling). It then maps these onto five information concepts: needs, exposure, legitimation, routes and opportunities. No estimation is performed.
extraction.identification_strategy: Not applicable. The article makes no causal or statistical identification claim.
extraction.scope: Population: information exchange among individuals, groups, organizations and concepts. Examples include library interlibrary-loan networks, hypertext subjects, co-workers, doctors, and East York residents. Institutional setting: libraries and information services, with a practitioner orientation. Era: mid-1990s, citing WWW, e-mail and online journals as new access routes (printed p. 330).

limitations: The article has no limitations section. Its own stated constraints are the following: whole-network designs need responses from all members, and the number of possible ties grows as n(n-1), so researchers are often limited in actors or relationships (printed pp. 328-329). Incomplete-data methods exist but are cited, not applied (Stork & Richards 1992).
Strength measures are context-dependent and vary by what is studied, where and whom (printed pp. 327-328). Dichotomizing ties by a frequency threshold discards strength information (printed p. 327).
Reported ties can be asymmetric: A may report many contacts with B while B reports few (printed pp. 326-327).

No empirical test is reported for the article's claims. Examples come from other studies or are hypothetical (health-information example; n=20 arithmetic). Recommendations for librarians (e.g., reorganizing circulated documents, rearranging routes) are not evaluated (printed pp. 330-331, 334, 340).
Research relying on titles or existing routes is said to miss new developments (printed pp. 339-340). This is a normative argument, not a tested finding.
The text is a 1996 conference paper and reflects mid-1990s technologies (printed p. 330).
Source PDF text layer is OCR-garbled in places (e.g., printed pp. 325, 332, 337), so some quoted text here is unreliable.

summary_md:
Haythornthwaite's article (LISR 18:323-342; the printed header says 1998, and it began as a 1996 ALISE talk) is an expository introduction to social network analysis. It has no data, sample or identification strategy. It defines a relationship by three attributes: content, direction and strength. A tie between two actors bundles all the relationships they maintain. Strength can be kept as a value or cut at a frequency threshold, and the article warns that cutting it at a threshold throws information away. It sets out five principles (cohesion, structural equivalence, prominence, range and brokerage) and the standard measures: density, centralization, cliques, degree, closeness, betweenness and block modelling. Its Figure 3 shows why betweenness can capture brokerage that degree misses. Drawing on Coleman, Katz and Menzel (1966), it separates sources that inform from close ties that legitimate adoption. It also argues that information becomes useful only when someone forwards it.

For Paul's systems this is a vocabulary paper, not evidence. No number in it carries over. Its real use is as a checklist against the graphs as built:
- **Direction.** The R Stage 3 scrape keeps sponsor-to-cosponsor direction. The AUG workbook sorts each edge's keys and `load_network` averages the two directions, so the cascade kernel runs on an undirected graph.
- **Strength.** Edges are valued (original cosponsor 1.0, regular 0.5, scaled by 1/sqrt of the bill's cosponsor count), which fits the article's advice not to cut strength at a threshold.
- **Multiplexity.** A pair that is tied in several channels never gets a stronger tie. Media edges are admitted only for untied pairs on the CU graph, or take the larger of the two weights under the holistic config.
- **Brokerage.** Betweenness exists only inside the retired InfluenceScore. The staffer graph measures diversity across node kinds, not structural holes.

The informing-versus-legitimating split is a loose conceptual parallel to the engine's two-factor kernel: one factor for diffusion, one for pressure. All bearings below are UNVERIFIED single-path readings (DE-062).

paul_entries.text:
Haythornthwaite, Caroline. “Social Network Analysis: An approach and technique for the study of Information Exchange.” *Library & Information Science Research*, vol. 18, no. 4, Sept. 1996, pp. 323–342, [https://doi.org/10.1016/s0740-8188(96)90003-1](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0740-8188(96)90003-1).

This article is the foundational study of the Social Network Analysis method, providing an original overview of its methodology, reasoning, and empirical workings. By dissecting the method of how it works, various relationships ultimately leading to a causal outcome, Social Network Analysis can be applied empirically, with an almost unlimited variation of data collection, to different domains. When applying the method across domains, the article notes that one must consider how the general availability of information affects the ultimate validity of the structure, which is particularly important in the field of politics, where word of mouth and behind-closed-doors dealings are common. Finally, it emphasizes the directionality and structure of the ultimate social network as paramount when examining emerging leaders, trends, and overall findings. While the article is excellent at viewing social networks from a theoretical perspective, it is thin on how to construct graphs and build data pipelines, likely due to its age. Diagnosis: Priority – Medium – Theory

bearings.paper_claim: Relationships carry three attributes: content, direction and strength. A pair is tied by all the relationships it maintains. Strength can be carried as the value of a link, or considered within a presence-absence dichotomy by requiring a minimum frequency. Reported directed ties can be asymmetric, with the two sides reporting different amounts. The article does not say that thresholding discards strength.

bearings.system_side: Stage 3 builds sponsor-to-cosponsor edges summed per (From,To). Weight = role (1.0 original, 0.5 regular) times f_bill, where f_bill = success multiplier (3.0 if the bill passed its origin chamber, else 1) x bill decay weight x size norm (1/sqrt C under the default dial). moneyball_core NETWORKS cu config sets symmetrize True, so the cu cascade loader mean-symmetrizes each pair; holistic_norm keeps direction. The AUG workbook re-keys edges as (min,max); load_network_directed reads the BASE vintage.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The article gives design principles and no estimate. It does not address 2:1 role weights, the success multiplier, the decay factor or the sqrt size norm, and it does not show that symmetrizing changes diffusion. It is not evidence for keeping or dropping regular-cosponsor edges, so the rejected drop must not be defended from this paper. Asymmetric reports are a survey feature, not a graph-construction rule.

Analyst wrongly said the article holds that thresholding discards strength; the article says a threshold can still reflect strength in a dichotomy and does not say it discards it. The inference that the paper is consistent with keeping regular-cosponsor edges is not in the text. Code path verified.

extraction.title: A Network-Based Measure of Cosponsorship Influence on Bill Passage in the United States House of Representatives
extraction.year: 2024 (arXiv v1, June 2024; this file is v2, revised 23 Nov 2025)
extraction.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.19554v2 [cs.SI]. Metadata hint confirmed: title, authors, arXiv ID all match the PDF header.
extraction.document_type: arXiv preprint; empirical political network analysis (no peer-review status stated in text)
extraction.coverage: Read in full: _text/139df50e52fc.txt lines 1-970 (printed pp. 1-26, through the full reference list). Annotation JSON read in full: 44 markup items, all pages 2-26. Figures 1-7 are present only as captions and axis labels in the extracted text, so plotted values are not available; figure-based numbers below come from the text. The text file ends at printed p. 26; no content was skipped.
extraction.research_question: Does a legislator-influence measure built from House bill cosponsorship, where two members accrue influence when a bill they both cosponsor passes and that influence decays over time, help explain which House bills pass? Does it beat conventional centralities (eigenvector, closeness, strength) as a signal of bill passage? (Sec. 1, pp. 1-2; Sec. 4-5, pp. 5-18)
extraction.theory: Influence accrues between legislators through repeated mutual cosponsorship of bills that pass (quid pro quo / logrolling, social capital, homophily, alliance formation; pp. 3-4). Influence capital accumulates with tenure and decays when a member is inactive (p. 7). Bill-level influence is meant to capture the 'influentials' idea that a few very influential people drive opinion and decisions (p. 13, citing Weimann [49] and Watts and Dodds [51]).
extraction.data: US House of Representatives bills, 111th-115th Congresses (Jan 2009 to Jan 2019), from ProPublica bulk bill data (ref [39]). Member IDs completed from Congress Legislators, Stewart and Woon, and McCrain data (refs [40-42]). Only bills are kept; simple, concurrent and joint resolutions are excluded (p. 4). Passage means success through introduction, committee and debate stages in the House, irrespective of Senate or enactment (p. 5). Units: bill (bill-level influence scores), legislator-month (influence I[t,i]), and legislator-pair-month (C tensors). N is not reported as a total bill count or member count anywhere in the text; only percentages appear. Table 1 (p. 7): share of House-originated bills passing in the House, Congresses 111-115: 10.98%, 7.3%, 9.8%, 11.84%, 13.49%. Share enacted into law: 3.87%, 2.96%, 3.55%, 3.31%, 3.84%. Mean cosponsors per bill: 21.50, 21.44, 21.96, 20.93, 19.01 (max 419, 425, 379, 332, 381). Mean bills per cosponsor: 235.72, 205.63, 227.45, 243.53, 250.87 (max 797, 632, 666, 695, 791). Text also states at least 87.85% of House bills had cosponsors in each term (p. 4). Median House passage time 98 days, mean 148 days (p. 11). Roughly 3% of all bills in the ProPublica data were enacted (p. 5). Bills are about 70% of proposed legislation (p. 5).
extraction.method: 1) Build monthly undirected weighted cosponsorship tensors: A[t,i,j]pass counts bills introduced in month t that include i and j as sponsor/cosponsors and eventually pass the House; A[t,i,j]tot counts all such bills (p. 6). Edges are symmetric; sponsorship and cosponsorship are treated equally (pp. 5-6). 2) Exponential decay with half-life 6, 12 or 24 months (k = ln(0.5)/half-life), cumulated monthly: C[t,i,j] = sum over n<=t of e^{k(t-n)} A[n,i,j] (Eq. 1-2, pp. 7-8). 3) Party-normalized influence: P[t,i]Dems and P[t,i]Reps are the decayed pass/total ratio summed over co-party members divided by party size (Eq. 3, p. 8). I[t,i] = P_Dems + P_Reps (Eq. 4, p. 8). 4) Bill influence at introduction month t_k: mean or max of I[t_k,i] over cosponsors C_k (Eq. 5, p. 10). 5) Compare passed vs failed bills in non-overlapping 4-month windows via relative difference = (mean passed minus mean failed) / mean failed (pp. 11, 13). Comparators: eigenvector centrality of D = C_pass / C_tot on the largest connected component, eigenproblem D x = lambda x (Eq. 6-7, pp. 15-16); closeness and strength centrality on the same LCC, Appendix A (Eq. 8-9, p. 18). Analysis is descriptive: plots, means and standard errors. No regression, no controls, no formal significance test is reported.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The paper makes an associational claim: bill-level influence separates passed from failed bills. No control for bill topic, committee, sponsor or party beyond the party-normalized score construction (the authors list topic and committee as future controls, p. 17). Two features of the construction bear on how the separation should be read. (a) Authors' stated choice (p. 10, lines 417-422): a bill is included in its own influence calculation, so the outcome of the bill being scored can enter its own predictor; authors argue the effect is at most one bill in a large numerator. (b) As written in Sec. 4 (p. 6, 'eventually pass (including possibly in month t)'), A[n] counts a bill as passing whenever it eventually passes, so C[t] can include passage events that happen after month t. The authors do not discuss whether this is look-ahead. This is a reader's reading of the definitions, not a claim the paper makes.
extraction.scope: Population: House-originated bills in the 111th-115th Congresses only. Institution: US House of Representatives; Senate, resolutions and enactment are excluded by design (pp. 4-5). Era: January 2009 to January 2019, which the authors tie to rising polarization after 2015 (p. 9, p. 13). Findings are aggregate; the authors explicitly decline to make claims about individual legislators (p. 17).

key_findings.finding: Passed bills have larger bill-level influence than failed bills in every 4-month period from 2009 to 2019, for both mean and max aggregation.
key_findings.numbers: Consistent separation in all 4-month windows; no per-window counts given.

key_findings.finding: Max-cosponsor influence separates passed and failed bills more than mean-cosponsor influence.
key_findings.numbers: Mean relative difference at 6-month half-life: 0.248 (max) vs 0.139 (mean).

key_findings.finding: The max-vs-mean separation holds at longer half-lives.
key_findings.numbers: 12-month half-life: 0.223 (max) vs 0.122 (mean). 24-month half-life: 0.203 (max) vs 0.109 (mean).

key_findings.finding: Half-life choice between 6 and 24 months barely changes discrimination; shorter decay gives slightly larger separation.
key_findings.numbers: Max-influence relative differences 0.248 / 0.223 / 0.203 for 6 / 12 / 24 months; standard errors 0.0139 / 0.0119 / 0.0107.

key_findings.finding: Eigenvector centrality is a much weaker indicator of passage than the influence measure.
key_findings.numbers: Mean relative difference 0.004 (mean eigenvector) and 0.002 (max eigenvector), vs 0.139 and 0.248 for influence.

key_findings.finding: Closeness and strength centrality are also weak indicators, and the authors attribute the failure to dense networks (untested).
key_findings.numbers: Closeness: 0.004 mean, 0.002 max. Strength: 0.004 mean, 0.003 max.

key_findings.finding: Legislator influence scores are small and their distribution mean does not rise over time; the authors hypothesize less collaboration in Congresses 114-115.
key_findings.numbers: Legislator scores range roughly 0 to 0.008. Distribution mean is smallest in Congresses 114 and 115.

key_findings.finding: Bill-level influence declines steeply from about 2015; the authors hypothesize this tracks rising polarization (not tested).
key_findings.numbers: No numeric decline reported in text.

key_findings.finding: Authors' interpretive conclusion: a bill is more likely to pass when one very influential member cosponsors it than when several moderately influential members do. This rests on the max-vs-mean comparison.
key_findings.numbers: Based on the 0.248 (max) vs 0.139 (mean) relative differences at 6-month half-life.

limitations: Authors state the influence notion is simplistic: all legislators are treated identically despite differing external influences and goals (p. 17, lines 650-654).
Results are aggregate only; authors decline to comment on legislator-level rankings because they have more confidence in aggregates (p. 17).
Bill topics, committee assignments and other factors that affect votes are not controlled; authors list this as future work (p. 17).
Influence is symmetric; asymmetric sponsor-to-cosponsor influence is left to future work (p. 7).
Aggregation uses 4-month non-overlapping windows; other windows and overlapping windows are not explored (p. 11).
Only House passage is studied; passage in the originating chamber is the outcome, and enacted-into-law outcomes are not analyzed (pp. 4-5).
Authors call the cosponsorship-derived influence measure 'only a proxy' for legislator influence (p. 17).
Comparison with the legislative-effectiveness score (LES) is not performed (p. 18).
Other network measures (e.g. network efficiency) and polyadic influence are not examined (p. 18).
Explanation for centralities failing (dense networks) is stated as a suspicion, not tested (p. 19).
Authors state no competing interests; funding from UC Presidential Postdoctoral Fellowship (Declarations, p. 22). Code is public at github.com/sarahsotoudeh/LegislativeInfluence (p. 1, p. 22).

summary_md:
Sotoudeh, Porter and Krishnagopal (arXiv 2406.19554v2) build a pairwise influence score from House cosponsorship covering the 111th to 115th Congresses (2009 to 2019). Each pair's share of jointly cosponsored bills that passed the House is decayed exponentially (half-lives of 6, 12 or 24 months), summed over co-party members and normalized by party size. A bill's influence is then the mean or the max of its cosponsors' scores at introduction. In every non-overlapping 4-month window, passed bills score higher than failed ones. The max-cosponsor score separates them better than the mean (relative difference 0.248 vs 0.139 at a 6-month half-life). Half-life barely matters (0.248 / 0.223 / 0.203). Eigenvector, closeness and strength centralities computed on the same pass/total matrix barely separate passed from failed bills (0.002 to 0.004). The analysis is descriptive only: no controls, no significance tests and no strata. A bill counts toward its own score, and as the formulas are written, edges can include passage that happens after the scoring month.

For Paul's system there are three points. First, the paper is cited as the source of the CU cosponsor network's edge weights, but the built weights depart from it on nearly every parameter: an additive ×3 success multiplier instead of a pass/total ratio, a per-Congress 0.8 decay (half-life of about 6 years), a 1/sqrt(C) size discount, unequal role weights and no party normalization. Second, the centrality result backs retiring direction-blind centrality from the Influence pillar. It also shows that any check of InfluenceScore against bill passage would be circular, because the edges are already weighted by passage. Third, code comments and brain notes cite the paper for claims it never tests, namely recruitment chains and influence versus cosponsor count. Paul's 6-month half-life note is also a mis-transfer: the paper's decay applies to accruing cosponsorship influence, not to stance salience.

bearings.paper_claim: Influence accrues per legislator pair as a decayed ratio C_pass / C_tot of mutually cosponsored bills that eventually pass the House. Sponsor and cosponsor are treated identically, edges are undirected, decay is monthly with half-life 6, 12 or 24 months, and scores are normalized by party size (Eq. 1-4). Passage means House passage. The authors call the result only a proxy (p. 17).
bearings.system_side: Brain cites this paper for the CU cosponsor edge weights. Code (congress_member_scraper.R lines 1776-1788 and 1923-1936; fec/network/build_holistic_base.py) builds weight = role (original 1.0, regular 0.5; holistic regular 0.2) x 3.0 if the last action matches the passage regex x 0.8 per Congress of age x 1/sqrt(C), summed per directed sponsor-to-cosponsor pair. This is a volume-weighted success boost, not a pass/total ratio, with no party normalization. Last-action caveat (build_holistic_base.py, 2026-08-17): 2,652 of 37,076 tie-contributing bills carry 39,390 of 410,411 ties (about 9.6 percent); scoring them as passed would raise unrolled tie weight about 14.9 percent.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports only the general idea of weighting ties by joint passage, for House bills 2009-2019 with House passage as outcome. It gives no evidence for the x3 multiplier, the 1/sqrt(C) discount, the 2:1 or 5:1 role ratio, the per-Congress decay, Senate ties or CU-topic bill universes. Read the citation as inspired by, not implements.

Summary 14.9 percent figure misread the caveat (it is the rise in tie weight, not the affected share), corrected here. Summary additive wording for the x3 factor corrected here.

extraction.document_type: Journal article: conceptual decision-model framework with a descriptive case study and simulation-style illustrations (no inferential statistics)
extraction.coverage: Entire extracted text file read (lines 0 to 838 of 0970f83c9875.txt, all chunks): front matter, highlights, abstract, Sections 1 to 5, CRediT, acknowledgements, references, and ScienceDirect page chrome. extraction.research_question: Stated objective (Sec. 1, p. 3 of the text, "Introduction"): "the objective of this study is to check the usefulness of the development and implementation of an integrative management information system." The abstract frames it as whether a Big Data-assisted social media analytics model (BD-SMAB) can help decision-makers with marketing strategy and competitive analysis. No explicit hypotheses or formal research questions are stated.
extraction.theory: No formal social-science theory. Foundations are knowledge management (KM) and business decision-making, plus the OMG Decision Model and Notation (DMN) standard for modeling decisions (Sec. 2 and Sec. 3). The decision procedure is a sequence of stages (intelligence, design/planning, choice/production of options, implementation). Stage naming is inconsistent: Sec. 3 (around line 162) says "information stage, conceptual design, development, and implementation stage," while later text describes intelligence, planning, produce options, and implementation. Sentiment and burst-detection components draw on text-mining and time-series methods, not a behavioral theory.
extraction.data: Case study (Sec. 3.1): 882,371 tweets about five retail businesses, collected via the Twitter search API by VOZIQ, a social media analytics firm one author collaborated with. Unit: individual tweets and comments. Time period is not stated. Sec. 4 software/performance evaluation: company fan pages of FMCG firms on Facebook, six brands, with household-panel purchase data mentioned (sample size and panel size not reported). Fig. 6 refers to ten brands. Table 1: Costco product and service categories (positive comment % and mean %). Table 2: share of social media mentions for five companies (Wal-Mart 35%, Costco 24%, Home Depot 19%, Kmart 11%, Kohl's 11%). The company set is inconsistent across the text: Sec. 3.1 names Costco, eBay, Kohl's, Hardware Depot, Amazon (line 249), and later Costco, Kohls, Walmart, Kmart, Habitat Depot (line 261). N for the Sec. 4 analyses is not reported.
extraction.method: Conceptual framework plus a descriptive case study. Components: (1) DMN-style decision modeling in two layers, decision requirements diagrams and decision logic (Sec. 2 and 3); (2) sentiment and phrase classification: Affin lexicon phrase scores, ensemble machine-learning classifiers on hybrid features to label praise vs complaint, and nonnegative matrix factorization for clustering (Sec. 1, around lines 125 and 129); (3) a linear model relating market value changes to weighted phrase/search-intensity changes, ΔC(t+1)=Σ w_k Δx_k(t) (Eq. 1), with weights estimated under an L1 penalty λΣ|w_k| (Eq. 2; the text writes "argmax" but a penalized least-squares minimization is described); (4) z-score normalization of 1-day variations over trailing n-day windows (Eq. 3; n=5 and 25 mentioned, burst threshold |z|>30); (5) burst detection on term frequency, a term co-occurrence/cross-correlation graph (threshold 0.1), Louvain community detection, and an event hotness index He(t)=Σ sentiment×volume over bursting events (Eq. 5); (6) Leximancer concept mapping and VOZIQ category/sentiment dashboards for the case study (Sec. 3.1). Eq. (1) and Eq. (2) are garbled in the extraction, so exact notation should be checked against the PDF.
extraction.identification: None. There is no causal identification strategy, no train/test or holdout design, no baseline comparison, no significance testing, and no robustness checks. Claims of superiority ("highest accuracy") are not tied to any measured metric.
extraction.scope: Population and setting: social media posts (mainly Twitter, Facebook) about large US-style retail companies (named in text; country not stated explicitly), plus FMCG brands on Facebook. Motivating domains listed in the abstract and conclusion include real estate, organizations, beauty trade fairs, finance, medicine, e-commerce. These are asserted, not analyzed. Era: circa 2021 publication; data period not reported. Institution: Chinese universities (author affiliations); VOZIQ is the commercial partner.

summary_md:
Zhang et al. (2022) propose BD-SMAB, a conceptual decision-support framework for business competitive analysis built from social media. It chains together several standard pieces: DMN decision modelling; Affin-lexicon and ensemble-classifier labelling of praise versus complaint; NMF clustering; an L1-penalised linear model of market-value change on phrase-intensity change (Eqs. 1-2); z-scored one-day burst detection over trailing 5- and 25-day windows (|z|>30); a term co-occurrence graph (cross-correlation >= 0.1) partitioned with Louvain; and a hotness index He(t), the sum of sentiment times volume over bursting events. The case study covers 882,371 tweets about five retailers, collected by VOZIQ, a commercial partner one author worked with. Its outputs are descriptive only: Costco category positive shares (jewelry 91%, parking 39%) and mention shares (Wal-Mart 35%, Costco 24%; window and denominator not stated). The paper has no holdout, no baseline and no metrics. Its "highest accuracy" claim has no numbers behind it. The authors call the framework conceptual. The company list is inconsistent, the equations are garbled, and several citations are wrong (the Affin citation points to a photonics paper).

For Paul's systems this is a weak, context-level source. The closest overlaps are methodological. Louvain on a thresholded correlation graph is what press_hcoi.py already does, using Malaterre's 0.6 threshold. A volume-and-sentiment burst index is a possible time-varying trigger for the salience-shock engine, whose uncertainty and polarization terms are currently static and estimated from the stance matrix. The paper does not validate any of these components, so nothing in it can justify changing a threshold, half-life or weight. Any idea taken from it starts out UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: Builds a term co-occurrence graph from cross-correlation of burst vectors (edge threshold 0.1) and partitions it with Louvain to find event communities; no modularity, stability or external-validity figure is reported.
bearings.system_side: HCoI builds member press-category profiles (recency-weighted), links pairs at Pearson >= 0.6 (Malaterre's threshold, env HCOI_CORR) and runs Louvain with seed 7, keeping communities of at least 3. Homophily replication at press resolution was null.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The pipeline shape is the same (correlation, threshold, Louvain), but the nodes are terms, not legislators, and the threshold (0.1 vs 0.6) is unjustified and unvalidated. That gives no grounds to retune HCOI_CORR or to read the null homophily result differently. Malaterre remains the governing source.

bearings.paper_claim: Defines a time-varying event hotness index He(t) = sum over bursting events of sentiment x volume, with bursts flagged by z-scores of one-day variation over trailing 5- and 25-day windows (|z|>30). It is proposed as a brand-value measure, and no estimates or forecast errors are reported.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3, Eqs. 3 and 5; contributions list line ~137
bearings.system_side: Salience parameters (partisan gap z_c, policy uncertainty psi_c, backfire b) are estimated from the static stance matrix. There is no time-series trigger for when an issue becomes salient. Go-public advice is computed per issue, not per moment.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A burst detector on press and social volume per CU category could supply a dated salience-onset signal. Any such signal stays UNVERIFIED until it is tested against Noble-Turner style co-partisan shifts on a second path. The paper's 'sentiment x volume' must not be imported as an influence or importance score: it measures volume, not access or influence. It comes from consumer tweets about retailers, not congressional statements.

bearings.paper_claim: Scores phrase sentiment with the general-purpose Affin lexicon plus an ensemble classifier for praise vs complaint. Accuracy is described as 'highest' with no metric, and the Affin citation points to an unrelated photonics paper.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 1, around lines 125-129; Sec. 4 lines 303, 335; reference list
bearings.system_side: Tone intensity is the LSD2015 charge (pos+neg)/words with negation handling, used as intensity only. Direction comes from the stance readers.
bearings.transfer_conditions: There is no evidence here that a general lexicon measures tone validly on congressional press releases. The open question (does LSD intensity agree with human-coded intensity?) is untouched. Rice & Zorn's case for domain dictionaries remains the relevant source.

gaps_exposed: No time-series burst or onset detection on press/social volume per CU category. Salience and media-blend treat attention as static or exponentially decayed (2.0-year press, 0.5-year social half-lives), so the system cannot date when an issue spiked. The paper names the gap but does not show it matters.

Social posts enter the media blend by platform-agnostic p80 scaling. The paper's claim that Facebook and Twitter indices differ (values only in Fig. 5) suggests platform effects could be checked. It is unvalidated, so this is a question, not evidence.
flags: The paper's 'highest accuracy' superiority claim has no metric, baseline or holdout. Do not cite it as validation for any sentiment or stance reader. Anything adapted from it stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

The hotness index He(t) sums sentiment x volume and is framed as a brand-value measure. Importing it as an influence, importance or closeness score would breach the wording rules (graph and volume scores are heuristic model outputs, not influence; D-025). Mention shares (Wal-Mart 35% etc.) have no stated window or denominator.

Conflict of interest: the case-study data came from VOZIQ, a commercial firm one author collaborated with, and no independence statement appears. The company list is inconsistent across sections. Several references are miscited (Affin -> photonics paper; duplicate Gheisari entries). Verify any citation before relying on it.
The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, so neither rejected SNA proposal is triggered.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper, and it appears in none of his component positions. The closest is his press-pillar position: he wants press statements, news cycles and social feeds, scored by sentiment, added as determinants of pathway change (the Bacik augmentation). This paper shares that aspiration in a business setting but gives no evidence that sentiment-scored social volume predicts anything, legislative or commercial. It neither supports nor undercuts his takeaway. It is a framework sketch, and it sits in the same genre as Taherdoost & Madanchian 2023, which Paul cites only for context. His notes are not made stale by it. The system's existing stance (sentiment is not stance; volume is not influence) is stricter than anything in this paper.

related.why: Both threshold a correlation graph and run Louvain to find communities. Malaterre supplies the 0.6 threshold press_hcoi.py actually uses. Zhang uses 0.1 on burst vectors and gives no validation.
Hargittai shows that big data from social network sites carries sampling biases. Zhang treats 882,371 tweets as representative of consumer sentiment and never examines who posts.
Rice & Zorn argue that general sentiment lexicons misfire on specialised vocabularies. Zhang applies the general Affin lexicon to retail tweets with no domain check.
Gives the methodological grounding for Twitter collection and its limits that Zhang's Twitter-API case study omits.

extraction.document_type: Empirical methods paper (proof of concept), research article with a single case study. Open Data and Open Materials badges. Code and datasets on Zenodo, doi 10.5281/zenodo.7967417.
extraction.coverage: Full text read in two passes (extracted text lines 1-933, through the reference list and the final footer). Paul's markup: all 86 annotation items in _annots/f0f9356bb79c.json were reviewed (63 cover policy/SNA framing and method; 1 cover the Table 2 and empty highlights). Covered text is paraphrased in paul_markup, not quoted, under the reproduction limit; the verbatim covered text stays in the source JSON. All 86 items are highlights with empty note content, so there are no sticky-note comments. Colour counts: yellow 64, green 15, purple 4, pink 3. Page numbers use the journal's e5-N labels, which match the PDF page numbers used by the annotations.
extraction.research_question: Can communities of actors who share similar semantic content ("hidden communities of interest", HCoIs) be recovered from the texts those actors produce when relational (social tie) data are absent, and can their evolution over time be traced as community genealogies?
extraction.theory: Actors' shared topical content is treated as a relational proxy: "who-talks-about-the-same-things-as-who" (Section 4, p.15). The HCoI networks are described as capturing ties mediated by texts rather than actual social ties. Grounding is in SNA, semantic network approaches (Carley 1993; Danowski 2011), and topic modelling. No formal theory of influence, persuasion or behaviour is stated.
extraction.data: Corpus of 16,917 full-text English-language research articles from eight philosophy-of-science journals (Table 1, p.5), published 1930-2017. Assembled in Malaterre and Lareau (2022). Unit of analysis for the topic model is the article; the network nodes are authors. Authors N = 8,009, with co-authored articles split equally across authors. Four periods of roughly 21 years each: 1930-1951, 1952-1973, 1974-1995, 1996-2017 (p.4). Article counts rise from 1,575 to 8,300 (5.3-fold); author count rises about eightfold; multi-authored share rises from 4% to 16% (p.5). About 65% of authors publish only once; the share of new authors per period is above 80% but declining (p.5-6). Lexicon after POS filtering (nouns, verbs, adverbs, adjectives; TreeTagger, Penn tags) and removal of words in fewer than 50 sentences: 23,672 terms (p.4, p.14). Abstract N = 16,917 refers to articles, not authors.
extraction.method: 1) Latent Dirichlet allocation (Blei et al. 2003; Griffiths and Steyvers 2004) on full articles via Gensim, k = 25 topics. k chosen as a compromise between Cv coherence (Roder et al. 2015) over k = 5-100 and manual inspection of top words; k above 35 gave no coherence gain (p.6, Fig. 3). Topics labelled manually into groups A-H (p.7-8, Table 2). 2) Each article's topic distribution is averaged per author per period, weighted by authorship share, giving author topic profiles (p.9). 3) Pearson correlations between author profiles within each period; correlation networks built in Gephi with default Louvain community detection. Authors with weighted publications above 2 retained; correlation threshold 0.6 (p.9). 4) Community topic profile = average of member author profiles (p.9). 5) Hellinger distances between community profiles across adjacent periods; closest pairings used for genealogies (p.9, p.13-14, Fig. 9). Descriptive network statistics computed in Gephi (Table 3, p.10). Inter-topic similarity = 1 minus Hellinger distance (p.7, Fig. 4).
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy; the paper is an unsupervised method. "Identification" of an HCoI means a Louvain community in a thresholded author correlation network. Validation is qualitative: communities and their change over time are judged consistent with the known history of the field (logical positivism; emergence of philosophy of biology in the 1970s; p.15, and Conclusion p.16). No ground-truth labels or held-out evaluation are reported.
extraction.scope: Population: authors of English-language articles in eight philosophy-of-science journals (including Philosophy of Science, Synthese, Erkenntnis, BJPS; Table 1). Era: 1930-2017. Not a policy corpus. The authors argue the approach applies to policy text (public health, international relations, voting, e-petitioning, citizen social-media text; p.3, p.16) but do not test it on policy data. The corpus is claimed to be representative of the discipline, while acknowledging that other venues and non-English publications are excluded (p.4).

key_findings.finding: A 25-topic LDA plus author correlation and Louvain pipeline recovers interpretable author communities with no relational data. Communities are labelled by their topic profiles.
key_findings.location: Abstract p.1; Section 2.2 p.6-9; Section 3.1 p.9-12
key_findings.numbers: k = 25; 16,917 articles; 8,009 authors; correlation threshold 0.6; authors with weighted publications > 2 kept

key_findings.finding: Network structure changes across eight decades. Density falls while modularity rises, so communities become more distinct and compact. Authors describe betweenness, cohesion and modularity as increasing, but cohesion is not monotone (see Table 3 check below).
The number of specialised communities roughly triples over the period, from 4 to 13.
key_findings.numbers: 4 communities (1930-51) to 13 (1996-2017), about 3.3-fold; authors describe this as threefold

key_findings.finding: Corpus growth is driven partly by growing co-authorship: multi-authored share rises, and articles per author stay roughly constant.
key_findings.numbers: Articles 1,575 to 8,300 (5.3-fold); authors about 8-fold; articles per author about 2 in each period; multi-authored share 4% to 16%

key_findings.finding: Topics map onto known philosophy-of-science themes, and inter-topic similarity is low overall. Only B-Arguments and H-History show notable similarity, about 0.4 with the other topics in their clusters.
key_findings.numbers: 25 topics in 8 groups (A-H); similarities near 0.4 for B-Arguments and H-History clusters

key_findings.finding: Genealogy: some communities persist across periods (logic and language, epistemology, philosophy of biology in later periods), some split or merge, and several appear with no clear predecessor. The 1974-95 period contains four novel communities.
key_findings.numbers: Four novel communities appear in 1974-95 without clear filiation (3c, 3f, 3h, 3i); philosophy of biology 2d shows little continuity with earlier communities; 1930s logical positivist cluster 1a maps to 2b

key_findings.finding: The authors read the findings as stabilisation after an early growth and diversification phase, and report that the output agrees with known episodes of the field. This is the only validation offered.
key_findings.numbers: No quantitative validation figure given

key_findings.finding: The method is computationally cheaper than semantic-network comparison. It uses three matrices, avoiding 8,009 semantic matrices of 23,672 x 23,672 and their pairwise distances.
key_findings.numbers: Matrices: author x topic 8,009 x 25; document x topic 16,917 x 25; topic x term 25 x 23,672. Avoided: 8,009 matrices and 8,009 x 8,009 / 2 pairwise comparisons

limitations: Authors state the methods work best with a monolingual corpus. For multilingual corpora they suggest machine-translating non-English texts into English (p.16, lines 688-693).

Authors state that the quality of HCoI networks depends on corpus representativeness, which is crucial for conclusions (p.16, lines 682-684). They acknowledge that philosophy of science is also published in other venues and in other languages (p.4).
Topic model choice: LDA was used, but any topic model is acceptable if topic assignments are continuous probabilities rather than crisp (p.16, lines 694-699).
The number of topics k is a compromise between coherence and human interpretability. Metrics alone do not settle k (p.6-8, lines 264-268, 311-313).
Topics depend on the modelled text, and corpus size and structure affect the choice of k and of units of analysis (p.8, lines 307-311).
HCoI networks are not social networks. Ties are mediated by texts, so they are a heuristic for possible real ties, not a substitute for them (p.15, lines 652-663).
Policy applicability is asserted but not tested in this paper (p.3, p.13, p.16).
Validation is qualitative and rests on consistency with expert knowledge of the field (p.15-16).

summary_md:
Malaterre and Lareau (Data & Policy 6, e5, 2024) is a proof of concept for finding "hidden communities of interest" (HCoIs) when no tie data exist. They fit a 25-topic LDA to 16,917 philosophy-of-science articles (1930-2017). They average each author's topic shares within each of four roughly 21-year periods. Authors with more than 2 weighted publications are kept, which leaves at most 8,009 authors. Authors are linked when the Pearson correlation of their profiles is at least 0.6, and Louvain then finds communities. Communities in adjacent periods are matched by Hellinger distance to trace their history. Over time, modularity rises (0.427 to 0.834), density falls (0.167 to 0.030), and the number of communities goes from 4 to 13. The only validation is that the results agree with the known history of the field. The authors also say plainly that HCoI ties are mediated by text and are a heuristic for possible real ties, not social ties. They argue the method suits policy text but do not test it on any.

For Paul's systems this paper is not new: it is the stated source of fec/network/press_hcoi.py, built on 2026-07-01. That script copies the pipeline almost step for step, except that it uses 19 regex-tagged CU press categories in place of LDA topics. Two system findings back the authors' own caveat. First, the HCoI layer was null for stance co-movement (49%). Second, it recovered only 4 of 41 cosponsor-isolated members. The paper therefore supports building the layer, but it does not support reading HCoIs as coalitions, as closeness, or as influence channels. Those are the readings the system's assumption text, Paul's annotation, and the holistic edge admission lean toward. Everything here is a single-agent reading and is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

Malaterre, Christophe, and Francis Lareau. “Inferring social networks from unstructured text data: A proof of concept detection of hidden communities of interest.” Data & Policy, vol. 6, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1017/dap.2023.48.

This article focuses on the methodological approach to turning unstructured data, such as long policy memos, into refined data that can be input as vectors and edges within a social network analysis graph. The main theory emphasizes the use of shared semantic content between seemingly unrelated groups using a fitted topic model. It provides a good foundational overview of how Social Network Analysis operates and how to craft your own framework. One potential extension of the current research is to infer the level of closeness between two congressional offices based on mapping their co-occurrences within texts or on general textual similarities—requiring a temporal element. Additionally, this topic model could be domain-specific to the trade association or consulting partner assigned to it. This also mentions Louvian community detection. Finally, note how they slimmed down the articles to increase computational efficiency. The author explicitly mentions this method in its application to advocacy. Diagnosis: Priority – Very High – Foundational

bearings.paper_claim: LDA k=25 on 16,917 articles; author topic profiles per roughly 21-year period, weighted by authorship share; keep authors with weighted publications above 2; Pearson r at least 0.6; Louvain (Gephi default); community profile = average of member profiles; genealogy by closest Hellinger pairing between adjacent periods; modularity 0.427 to 0.834 and communities 4 to 13.

bearings.system_side: press_hcoi.py follows the same steps but uses 20 curated regex-tagged press categories, not 19, in place of LDA topics. Each item's weight is split evenly over its labels and weighted by recency. r cutoff 0.6 (HCOI_CORR); MIN_W 3.0 as the transient-author filter; Louvain seed 7; communities under 3 members dropped; one median-date split into two periods; Hellinger matching; PERSISTS / drifts / NOVEL cutoffs 0.25 and 0.45. Stored data/stance/press_hcoi.json: 155 members profiled, 6 communities, 1900 edges, 20 categories.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Mechanics carry over. The evidence does not: the paper covers an 88-year academic corpus in four periods with over 80 percent new authors per period and only qualitative validation. Here the split is two half-periods of one press stream, so NOVEL and PERSISTS labels reflect the script's own thresholds. Quote member denominators as 155 profiled, not the 385 in the script docstring, which is stale.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side reproduced: k=25, 16,917 articles, 8,009 authors, weight above 2, r 0.6, Louvain, Hellinger matching, Table 3 modularity and community counts. System side wrong on category count: 20 entries in the CATEGORIES block of the R source and 20 categories in the stored artifact, not 19.

bearings.paper_claim: HCoIs are about who-talks-about-the-same-things-as-who. Links are mediated by texts, are not social ties, and serve as a heuristic for possible real ties. (The analyst gloss that communities are not labelled from alignment is not stated in the paper.)
bearings.system_side: profiles() in press_hcoi.py counts attention across categories only and never reads the stance column, so a community can in principle hold members on both sides of an issue. The coalition assumption text attributed to the paper sits in a component file that was not opened; the paper does not support reading HCoIs as coalitions. The 49 percent co-movement null is not reproduced (see the stance bearing).

bearings.verifier_note: Paper quote at lines 652-663 verified. Code verified: no stance input in profiles(). The H-5 membership example was not checked against an artifact.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper offers no evidence that text-similarity ties carry influence or transmission; it frames HCoI mapping as a heuristic for actual social connections that would still need confirmation.
bearings.system_side: build_multilayer_network.py admits HCoI edges at weight 0.6 x r x HCOI_W. HCOI_W defaults to 0.2, so 0.12 is the ceiling at r = 1 (a maximum from the formula, not a clamp in code), about 0.02 kernel probability per step. The CU config admits only edges touching a cosponsor-isolated member; the holistic dominance rule admits HCoI edges generally. The 857-edge holistic count and the 4 of 41 reconnection count were not reproduced. The stored press_hcoi.json D4 block reads 14 isolated members and 0 placed in a community.

summary_issues: The summary says press_hcoi.py was built on 2026-07-01. Git history for fec/network/press_hcoi.py starts at the 2026-07-02 baseline commit 62a209e2f, so the date is unconfirmed.
The 19 regex-tagged categories (summary, gap 3, bearing 5) are wrong: the R source and data/stance/press_hcoi.json both have 20 categories.
The HCoI stance co-movement null (49 percent) is not reproduced: stance_dynamics.json co_movement reads same 134, opposite 122 (52 percent), with no layer label.

The recovery figure of 4 of 41 cosponsor-isolated members is not reproduced from the current press_hcoi.json, whose D4 block reads 14 isolated and 0 placed in a community. Name the run or admission count before quoting it.
Gap 5 refers to 8 communities; the current press_hcoi.json has 6 (sizes 50, 42, 20, 19, 11, 7).
The 385-member denominator in the press_hcoi.py docstring is stale; the current artifact profiles 155 members (MIN_W 3.0).

The summary says density falls from 0.167 to 0.030, but density is not monotone (0.027 in 1974-95, then 0.030). Table 3 cohesion values (31,558; 18,876; 25,465; 41,115) and betweenness values cannot match their labels at N of about 8,009: density 0.167 implies average degree near 1,300. Do not quote those table values without checking the source table.
Gap 4 and the Ward bloc count of 9 are wrong: the default caps the bloc count at 8.
gaps_exposed: The HCoI layer has never been checked against a quantitative criterion. The open question of whether press-attention communities predict within-community cosponsorship above chance has not been answered. The paper also validates only qualitatively, so it offers no bar to borrow.

There is no signed HCoI variant (attention times stance sign). The current communities cannot tell allies from opponents who fight over the same issue, such as the H-5 CU-Bank defensive-fight cluster.

The 19-category regex taxonomy that feeds the profiles has no measured precision and no counterpart to the paper's coherence-based choice of k. The paper's requirement that topic assignments be continuous is only partly met, because each item's tags are crisp and split evenly.

The genealogy uses one median-date split into two periods, with PERSISTS / drifts / NOVEL cutoffs (0.25 / 0.45) that are not anchored in the paper. There is also no member-overlap check alongside the profile distance.
Louvain runs once with a single seed (7), and there is no seed or resolution stability check on the 8 communities.
There is no representativeness audit of who gets profiled (MIN_W 3.0) by party or chamber, even though collection coverage differs (D 92.5 vs R 87%; Senate 83 vs House 96%).
flags: The component's assumption text, 'Shared issue attention indicates coalition (Malaterre & Lareau 2024)', overstates the paper. The paper says HCoI ties are mediated by text, are not social ties, and are only a heuristic for possible real ties. Under D-025, HCoI communities and edges must be described as topical-similarity heuristics, never as coalition, closeness, or access.

Paul's takeaway, 'infer closeness between two congressional offices from co-occurrence or textual similarity', uses closeness language that D-025 bars and that the paper itself disclaims. A safer wording is 'topical-similarity heuristic between offices'.

Paul's note that the paper 'explicitly applies the method to advocacy' is not accurate. The paper argues the method could apply to policy and advocacy, but it tests only a philosophy-of-science corpus.

Under the holistic configs, the dominance admission rule (Paul's 2026-08-18 ruling) puts 857 HCoI similarity edges into the cascade kernel. The paper gives no evidence that such ties transmit influence. This is flagged as beyond the paper's evidence, not as a recommendation to reverse the ruling.
The PERSISTS / drifts / NOVEL genealogy labels come from the system's own thresholds, not from the paper. Treat them as UNVERIFIED descriptive labels (DE-062).
Caution when quoting the paper: its text says betweenness, cohesion and modularity all increase, but cohesion in Table 3 is not monotone. Quote the table values, not the prose.
The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, so neither rejected SNA proposal is implicated. LDA identity sources are also not involved.
paul_alignment: Paul's annotation agrees with the paper on method: shared semantic content becomes vectors, then correlation edges, then Louvain, with a time element. The system put this in place on 2026-07-01 (fec/network/press_hcoi.py) as a two-period Hellinger genealogy, so his note is stale. It still reads as a future extension, but it is built, and it has since produced two results his notes do not record. HCoI neighbours showed null stance co-movement (49%), and the layer reconnected only 4 of 41 cosponsor-isolated members under the CU config. His idea of a domain-specific topic model per trade association or client was carried out in a different form: a curated 19-category CU taxonomy instead of a per-client LDA, and that taxonomy has never been validated. Two parts of his reading go beyond the paper. One is the framing of office 'closeness', which conflicts with D-025 and with the authors' own heuristic caveat. The other is the claim that the paper 'applies' the method to advocacy, when it only argues that it could. His note that the authors 'slimmed down the articles' is partly right. Their efficiency comes from part-of-speech and frequency filtering of the lexicon, and from working with three small matrices instead of 8,009 semantic matrices.

related.why: Paul's cross-reference notes for Malaterre list Ardekani et al. for Louvain community detection. Ardekani builds communities from a relational legislative citation network; Malaterre builds them from text similarity alone. Link verified.

Aref partitions a signed network under generalized balance, which encodes agreement and disagreement. HCoI attention profiles carry no sign, so the two are complementary on alignment. The system counterpart named in the analyst output was not checked.

Pritoni's systematic review covers determinants of lobbying coalitions, including issue salience and brokers (both recur in the item). That is the coalition theory the HCoI-as-coalition reading would need, and Malaterre does not supply it.

Zhou models stance change on temporal interaction graphs (user-hashtag and user-user). Topical-similarity graphs do not carry the communication ties that modelling assumes. The 49 percent null the analyst cites is not reproduced, so the link should not lean on it.

Both are text-data resources for social scientists. Steinert-Threlkeld covers Twitter data acquisition and processing and does not treat politicians' text as relational data; representativeness is mentioned only briefly. Use only for data-collection caveats.

backlinks.why: Both papers were ingested in the same 2026-07-01 wave and both were ported to press text (Malaterre to HCoI shared-attention communities, Joo to duplication-rate frame alignment), so both share the source-author attribution exposure.

Malaterre infers ties from Pearson correlation of LDA topic profiles at a 0.6 threshold and then runs Louvain, the recipe press_hcoi.py implements. Zareie also uses Pearson correlation, but on structural neighbourhood vectors, and multiplies it by a direct common-neighbour term. The overlap is technique-level, not the same method.
Item exists. Baptista does not cite Malaterre. Analyst link only: the HCoI layer's added value is the kind of layer Baptista's overlap and ablation logic would test.

press_hcoi.py takes its method from Malaterre and Lareau (2024), which correlates text profiles. The article's relational view bears on attribute-based grouping, but it does not discuss text profiles, so no direct contradiction is shown.
Both threshold a correlation graph and run Louvain to find communities. Malaterre supplies the 0.6 threshold press_hcoi.py actually uses. Zhang uses 0.1 on burst vectors and gives no validation.
